questions.q: In the raw node:http server, JSON.parse threw inside the async request callback. Why did the client hang instead of getting an error response?
questions.explain: node:http calls your function and ignores what it returns. A rejected promise from it goes nowhere: no response is written, and without an unhandledRejection handler Node ends the process. The framework wraps every request in its own try/catch.
options: Nobody awaited the callback's promise, so the error became an unhandled rejection and no code ever wrote a response
JSON.parse returns undefined on bad input

questions.q: The raw server did { id: newId, ...JSON.parse(text) }. What went wrong when the client sent {"title":"Kindred","id":"b1","featured":true}?
questions.explain: Later properties in a spread win, so the client's id replaced the server's, and any extra field was stored. A strict schema that refuses unknown keys, and a record built from named fields, prevent it.
options: Nothing; the server chose the id
The client's id and featured overwrote and extended the record: mass assignment

questions.q: DELETE /books/b1 is sent to a router that only has GET /books/:id. What is the correct answer?
questions.explain: The resource exists; the method is not supported on it. 405 with Allow tells the client exactly what would work, which 404 would hide.
options: 405 Method Not Allowed, with an Allow: GET header

questions.q: Routes GET /books/:id and GET /books/new are registered in that order. Which one handles GET /books/new in the mini router, and why?
questions.explain: Registration order should not decide this, or adding a route in the wrong file silently breaks another. Scoring static segments above parameters makes the result predictable.
options: /books/:id with id = "new", because it was registered first
/books/new, because static segments are more specific and the routes are sorted by specificity

questions.q: Why does the router wrap decodeURIComponent in try/catch?
questions.explain: Any input the client controls can be malformed. Turning parser exceptions into client errors keeps the status honest and the error logs free of noise.
options: A broken percent-encoding such as %E0%A4%A makes it throw a URIError; that is the client's mistake and should be a 400, not a 500
It returns undefined for unknown characters

questions.q: Middleware [logging, auth, handler] run as an onion. In what order do their "after" parts run?
questions.explain: Each middleware wraps everything inside it, so the innermost finishes first. The outermost starts first and finishes last, seeing the final response.
options: Only the last one runs its "after" part

questions.q: A request-logging middleware is placed inside the error-handling middleware. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: The thrown error travels outward past the logger to the error handler. With the logger outside, it receives the response the error handler built, including the 4xx and 5xx ones you most need to see.
options: When a handler throws, the error skips the logger's "after" code, so failed requests are never logged

questions.q: Why does compose throw when a middleware calls next() twice?
questions.explain: A bug like "retry by calling next again" silently duplicates side effects. Failing loudly turns it into an error during development.
options: The rest of the pipeline, including the handler, would run twice: two orders, two charges
JavaScript does not allow calling a function twice
Because the second call would be too slow

questions.q: A maintenance middleware returns a 503 without calling next(). What happens to the handler?
questions.explain: Answering early is how authentication, rate limits and maintenance modes work: the inner layers are skipped, the outer ones still observe the response.
options: It runs after the 503 is sent
It never runs; the outer middleware still see the 503 on the way out
It runs first, then the 503 replaces its response

questions.q: What do you gain by describing the body once with s.object({...}) instead of writing an interface and a separate parser?
questions.explain: Infer<typeof NewBook> is computed from the schema. Change a field in one place and both the check and every handler's type change with it.
options: The runtime check and the TypeScript type come from the same description, so they cannot drift apart
The body no longer needs to be JSON
The client gets the TypeScript type

questions.q: Why does s.object refuse keys that are not in the shape, instead of silently dropping them?
questions.explain: Both choices prevent mass assignment. Refusing also tells an honest client about its mistake, which silently dropping hides.
options: A client sending role or id is either confused or attacking; a clear 400 surfaces client bugs and makes probing visible

questions.q: A handler throws TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'priceKobo'). What should the response body contain?
questions.explain: Internal messages reveal field names, file paths and library versions to attackers. The request id connects a user's report to the full log entry.
options: The error message, so the client can report it
A generic message and the request id; the details go to the log under that id

questions.q: Why does HttpError carry a code such as "conflict" besides the English message?
questions.explain: A client that compares messages breaks when someone fixes a typo. Codes are part of the API contract; messages are for people.
options: Clients can branch on a stable machine-readable code, while the message stays free to change or be translated

questions.q: A book was saved, then the newsletter listener threw. What should the client receive?
questions.explain: The bus isolates listeners with Promise.allSettled. Reporting a failure for a saved book would make the client retry and create a duplicate.
options: 201: the operation succeeded; the listener's failure is logged and handled separately

questions.q: When should a reaction to book.added go to a queue or outbox instead of the in-process bus?
questions.explain: In-process listeners run inside the request and die with the process. Durable, retryable work belongs in a queue, published reliably with an outbox.
options: When it is slow or must survive a crash, like sending e-mails or charging cards
When there is exactly one listener

questions.q: Why does readBody check the size while reading the chunks instead of after reading the whole body?
questions.explain: A limit that is enforced after the damage is not a limit. Counting as bytes arrive lets the server refuse with 413 early.
options: Checking afterwards means buffering the whole 2 GB first, which is exactly the memory exhaustion the limit exists to prevent

questions.q: A client sends title=Kindred with Content-Type: text/plain to an endpoint that expects JSON. Which status fits best?
questions.explain: 415 says "I cannot read this kind of body". 406 is about the response type the client accepts; 400 and 422 are for bodies in the right format with wrong content.

questions.q: The adapter opens a container scope per request and disposes it in finally. What does that give controllers?
questions.explain: The scoped controller and its scoped dependencies live exactly as long as the request. finally guarantees disposal, so a failed request cannot leak an open transaction.
options: They can depend on request-scoped objects (a transaction, the current user) that are created for this request and always cleaned up, even after an error
Nothing; scopes are only for tests

questions.q: What does server.close() do to a request that is still being handled?
questions.explain: That is why the in-flight /report still got its 200 during the stop. closeIdleConnections() additionally drops kept-alive connections that are doing nothing, so shutdown does not wait for them.
options: Lets it finish; it only stops accepting new connections, and its callback runs when the last connection ends
Nothing, and it also keeps accepting new connections

questions.q: Why do the examples and tests listen on port 0?
questions.explain: Hard-coded ports fail when two test runs, or a developer's other server, already use them. server.address().port tells you the real one.
options: Port 0 is the default HTTP port
The operating system picks a free port, so parallel tests never collide; the code then reads which port it got

questions.q: In @zudojs/http, what is ctx.request.body for a JSON POST?
questions.explain: The server cannot know whether bytes are JSON, a form or an image, so it gives you the bytes (within a size limit). Your mini framework made the opposite choice and parsed JSON for every request.
options: The raw bytes (a Uint8Array), which you decode and parse yourself

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Splitting on / produces empty strings for leading, trailing and doubled slashes; filtering them out normalises all these spellings to the same segments.
questions.code:
const split = (path: string) => path.split("/").filter((segment) => segment !== "");
console.log(split("/books/b1"), split("/books/b1/"), split("//books///b1"), split("/"));

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Parameters are decoded, so %20 becomes a space. A path with more segments than the pattern does not match, and a static segment must be equal.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each layer wraps the next: a starts first and finishes last, and its result wraps b's, which wraps the handler's.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: On Sunday the inner middleware answers 503 without calling next, so the handler never runs, but the outer logging middleware still records the 503.

questions.explain: The first body is valid. The second has three problems, and all three are reported: the refused id, the blank title and the fractional price.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Only deliberate HttpErrors reach the client with their message. Anything else, even a thrown string, is treated as a bug: a generic 500 with the request id.

questions.explain: allSettled waits for every listener and never rejects, so one failure cannot stop the others or the request. Promise.all would reject as soon as the newsletter failed.

questions.explain: The second body passes the 64-character limit on its second chunk (80 characters), and reading stops there: the last two chunks are never buffered.

questions.q: Write matchRoute(routes, method, path) returning "<name> {params}" for a match, "405 <allowed>" when only the method is wrong, and "404" otherwise. Parameters start with :. The program should print the four lines in the expected output.
questions.explain: The router remembers the methods of routes whose path matched, so it can tell "no such resource" (404) from "not with this method" (405, with the list for the Allow header).

questions.q: Write compose(middleware, handler) for the onion model: each middleware gets (ctx, next); calling next twice must throw next() called twice. The program should print the lines shown in the expected output.
questions.explain: last remembers the deepest index already entered; a second next() from the same layer asks for an index that is not deeper, which can only mean a repeat.
questions.expected:
logging in | auth in | handler | auth out 200 | logging out 200
next() called twice

questions.q: Write withBody(parse, handler): it runs parse(ctx.body); on failure it returns { status: 400, body: { error: "validation_failed", issues } } without calling the handler; on success it calls handler(ctx, value). The program should print the two lines in the expected output.
questions.explain: The generic T flows from the parser to the handler, so book is typed { title: string } without a cast, and the handler can never see an unchecked body.

questions.q: Write a typed EventBus<M> with on(name, listener) returning an unsubscribe function, and emit(name, payload) that runs all listeners with Promise.allSettled and returns the number that failed. The program should print the lines shown in the expected output.
questions.explain: After off() only the failing listener is left, so the second emit indexes nothing and still reports one failure. Wrapping each listener in an async function turns a synchronous throw into a rejection that allSettled can collect.

questions.q: Write allow(key, now) for a fixed-window limiter: at most 2 requests per key per 1,000 ms window; it returns true or false. The program should print true true false true true.
questions.explain: Ada's third request in her first window is refused; Tunde has his own window; at 1,000 ms Ada's window resets. Taking now as a parameter makes the limiter testable without waiting.
questions.starter:
// write allow(key, now)

console.log(allow("ada", 0), allow("ada", 100), allow("ada", 200), allow("tunde", 250), allow("ada", 1_000));

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The scores are compared as strings, character by character: "22" beats "212" at the second character, and "212" beats "21" because it is longer with the same start, then comes "12". Mixing lengths looks odd but is harmless: routes with different segment counts never compete for the same path, so only the order within one length matters. Equal scores keep their original order because the sort is stable.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: finally runs after the try or the catch, whichever ran, and before the code that follows. That is why the adapter disposes the request scope in finally: success or failure, it is cleaned up before the response is written.
options: handler ran, scope disposed, sent 200, error mapped, scope disposed, sent 500
handler ran, sent 200, error mapped, sent 500
handler ran, scope disposed, sent 200, error mapped, sent 500
handler ran, sent 200, scope disposed, error mapped, sent 500, scope disposed

questions.q: Write toResponse(error, requestId): an HttpError becomes its status with { error: code, message }; anything else becomes 500 with { error: "internal_error", requestId } and pushes "logged: <message or value>" to logs. The program should print the lines shown in the expected output.
questions.explain: The internal message reaches the log, never the client. The shared request id is what lets a support person connect the two.

questions.q: Write parseBody(text, contentType, limit) returning { status: 200, value }, or { status: 413 } when text.length exceeds limit, { status: 415 } when the type does not start with application/json, and { status: 400 } for invalid JSON. Check in that order. The program should print 200 413 415 400.
questions.explain: The cheapest checks come first: size before anything else, then the declared type, and only then the parse. A charset parameter after the media type is normal, which is why the check uses startsWith.
